concepts.title: Structural Chromosomal Abnormalities
concepts.definition: A chromosome can break and heal in four tell-tale ways: deletion trims a segment away as in retinoblastoma on chromosome 13, duplication repeats a stretch as in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease on chromosome 17, inversion flips a piece through 180 degrees leaving the length unchanged as in RCAD syndrome, and translocation moves a piece onto another chromosome - mutually as in Burkitt lymphoma between chromosomes 8 and 14, or one-way in the Robertsonian type that lowers the chromosome count.
concepts.key_idea: Shorter, longer, flipped or relocated - the breakage pattern names the aberration and points to the disease.
question_patterns: name the four structural chromosomal abnormalities and sketch each rearrangement
which disease follows deletion of part of chromosome 13 and which follows duplication on chromosome 17
differentiate reciprocal translocation from Robertsonian translocation with the Burkitt lymphoma example
why does an inversion leave chromosome length unchanged yet reorder the genes
what is a ring chromosome and how does it arise from two-ended deletion
match retinoblastoma Charcot-Marie-Tooth and RCAD syndrome with their chromosomal rearrangements

solution_steps.explain: Missing piece means deletion; repeated piece means duplication.
Same length but reversed gene order marks inversion.
A piece moving to a different chromosome is translocation - reciprocal if exchanged, Robertsonian if one-way.

worked_examples.q: Repeating a chromosome segment is called what: duplication or deletion?

concepts.title: Numerical Abnormalities and Polyploid Sets
concepts.definition: Whole chromosomes can be lost or gained: monosomy removes one of a pair, trisomy adds one, both counts of aneuploidy - as against polyploidy, where entire sets multiply so a human-count genome would hold 69 in triploid or 92 in tetraploid form; crop breeding exploits this, giving hexaploid bread wheat, tetraploid cabbages and mustards, triploid banana and apple, and octoploid strawberry and sugarcane.
concepts.key_idea: Add one for a trisomy, subtract one for a monosomy, and multiply the haploid number by set count for polyploids.
question_patterns: write the chromosome totals of a monosomic and a trisomic cell starting from the diploid number of 46
a triploid human-count genome would carry how many chromosomes - compute from 23 per set
how many chromosomes does a tetraploid cell with 23 per set contain
differentiate aneuploidy from polyploidy with one example of each
state the ploidy of bread wheat cabbage banana and sugarcane as used in food
which meiotic error produces trisomy and what is it called

solution_steps.explain: Trisomy adds a chromosome and monosomy removes one.
Each complete set holds the haploid number.

worked_examples.q: Losing one chromosome of a pair is called what: monosomy or trisomy?

concepts.title: Down Klinefelter and Turner Syndromes
concepts.definition: Three karyotypes anchor human cytogenetics: trisomy 21 gives Down syndrome with flat face, palmar crease and low IQ and one extra chromosome in 47,XX+21 or 47,XY+21; an extra X in 47,XXY males yields Klinefelter syndrome with tall stature, small testes and a single Barr body on buccal smear; and monosomy X in 45,X females gives Turner syndrome with short stature, webbed neck and no Barr body.
concepts.key_idea: Count the sex chromatin: one Barr body betrays the extra X of Klinefelter, none marks the missing X of Turner.
question_patterns: describe the origin symptoms and treatment of Down syndrome - which chromosome is repeated and why does maternal age matter
what karyotype and what Barr body pattern distinguish Klinefelter syndrome on a buccal smear
why cannot a Turner syndrome mother pass the condition to her daughters
differentiate the clinical pictures of Down Klinefelter and Turner syndromes
which nondisjunction event builds an XXY zygote from an XX ovum and a Y sperm
name two prenatal diagnostic techniques used for chromosomal syndromes

solution_steps.explain: 47,XX+21 or 47,XY+21 is Down; 47,XXY is Klinefelter; 45,X is Turner.
Normal male cells show none; Klinefelter shows one; Turner females show none.
Flat face and palmar crease for Down; tall stature and gynaecomastia for Klinefelter; webbed neck and absent menstruation for Turner.

worked_examples.q: Trisomy of which chromosome causes Down syndrome: 21 or 17?

concepts.title: Incidence Rates of Chromosomal Syndromes
concepts.definition: Each syndrome carries a headline frequency - about one Down baby per 800 live births, one Klinefelter male per 1000 newborn boys, and one Turner girl per 2500 newborn girls - so dividing a birth cohort by the rate predicts how many affected newborns a hospital or district should expect.
concepts.key_idea: Divide the birth total by each syndrome's rate denominator to forecast case counts.
concepts.textbook_ref: kebt108.txt section 8.1.2 (incidence lines of the three syndromes)
question_patterns: a hospital records 16000 live births - how many Down syndrome babies are expected at one per 800

solution_steps.explain: One case per 800 births sets the denominator.
One male case per 1000 newborn boys.

worked_examples.q: About one Down baby is born per how many live births: 800 or 8?

concepts.title: Monogenic Disorders and Pedigree Mapping
concepts.definition: Over ten thousand human illnesses trace back to a single faulty gene and therefore follow Mendelian rules, sorted by whether the mutant allele sits on an autosome or the X and by dominance - autosomal recessive sickle cell anaemia and cystic fibrosis, autosomal dominant achondroplasia and Huntington disease, X-linked recessive haemophilia and Duchenne dystrophy, X-linked dominant hypophosphatemia; a family tree drawn with standard pedigree symbols reveals which rule applies.
concepts.key_idea: One gene, four inheritance routes - autosomal or X-linked, dominant or recessive - and the pedigree tells you which.
question_patterns: classify sickle cell anaemia cystic fibrosis haemophilia and achondroplasia by their mode of inheritance
what do the standard symbols of a pedigree chart represent for males females affected individuals and mating
why does cystic fibrosis show more than 200 different mutations in one gene yet one disease

why are carriers of a recessive allele healthy yet able to transmit the disorder
how many humans are statistically estimated to carry defective recessive genes

solution_steps.explain: Note affected males versus females across generations and whether parents of affected children are unaffected.
Male-to-male transmission rules out X-linkage; skipping generations suggests recessivity; every generation affected suggests dominance.
Assign autosomal or X-linked, dominant or recessive, and predict carrier and risk statuses.

worked_examples.q: Sickle cell anaemia follows which inheritance: autosomal recessive or X-linked dominant?

concepts.title: Carrier Crosses in Recessive Disease
concepts.definition: Two healthy carriers of a recessive allele - each S/s at the sickle locus, say - gamete three genotype classes in their children: one quarter affected s/s, half carriers S/s, and one quarter clear S/S, so risk counselling for such couples starts from the quarter-and-half split.
concepts.key_idea: Quarter affected, half carriers, quarter clear - the fixed forecast of a carrier-by-carrier mating.
question_patterns: two carrier parents S/s plan four children - how many are expected affected with sickle cell anaemia and how many to be carriers

a carrier marries a homozygous normal partner - what fraction of children will be carriers
which regions of India show a high frequency of sickle cell anaemia

solution_steps.explain: Only the s/s combination falls ill, one of four combinations.
Two of the four combinations are healthy carriers.

worked_examples.q: In a carrier-by-carrier recessive cross, what fraction of children are affected: one quarter or all?

concepts.title: X-linked Transmission Probabilities
concepts.definition: Sex chromosomes give the transmission its asymmetry: a carrier mother passes a recessive X to half her sons, an affected father hands his X to every daughter but no son, and in the dominant form an affected mother likewise shares the trait with half of both her sons and daughters.
concepts.key_idea: Halve the children for sons, then halve again for those inheriting the affected X.
question_patterns: a carrier mother and a normal father expect five children - how many sons are predicted affected with an X-linked recessive disorder
why does an affected father in X-linked recessive inheritance pass the trait to none of his sons yet all daughters become carriers

which protein does the dystrophin gene encode and what fails in Duchenne muscular dystrophy
give two examples of X-linked dominant disorders in humans

solution_steps.explain: Half of any progeny are sons.
A carrier mother transmits the mutant X to half of her sons.

worked_examples.q: A carrier mother passes a recessive X to what fraction of her sons: half or none?

concepts.title: Polygenic Disorders and Mitochondrial Inheritance
concepts.definition: Several genes acting together produce the common chronic disorders - diabetes mellitus where type 2 makes up about ninety percent of cases against ten percent for insulin-dependent type 1, hypertension staged from 120 over 80 upward, and coronary heart disease built by atherosclerotic plaques; separately, mutated mitochondrial genes ride the egg alone, so severity tracks the mix of faulty and healthy mitochondria and only mothers transmit the disease.
concepts.key_idea: Nine of every ten diabetics are type 2; and a mitochondrial father transmits nothing - only the maternal line matters.
question_patterns: out of 400 diabetic patients how many are expected to be type 2 and how many type 1
differentiate type 1 from type 2 diabetes on the basis of beta cell damage and insulin requirement

why was coronary heart disease earlier called ischaemic heart disease - define atherosclerosis and ischemia
why can a father with a mitochondrial gene defect never pass it to his children
why do brain heart and muscle cells suffer most from mitochondrial gene defects

solution_steps.explain: Type 2 covers about ninety percent of diabetes cases.
Whatever is left of the cases is insulin-dependent type 1.

worked_examples.q: About what percent of diabetes cases are type 2: ninety or ten?
